- Real-time clinical note summarization and classification with P95 < 300ms for short prompts (≤ 512 tokens).
- Embedding-based search + reranker for patient notes (privacy-preserving) with nightly reindexing.
- Private deployment / Dedicated capacity with KMS + audit logs.

3) Embeddings workflow: batching, index architecture (FAISS + nightly re-ranker pass), and expected throughput for indexing and query-time reranking. Attachment: embedding-sample.jsonl.
4) Dedicated capacity sizing: initial baseline + scaling policy (autoscale triggers, max concurrency, queueing).
5) Security checklist for your InfoSec team — we can loop them into the next call.

Specific questions we still need from you to finalize the sizing:
- Peak QPS for generation vs. embedding queries (rough numbers, even ballpark).
- Expected average sequence length for the summarization flows (typical note sizes).
- Any compliance constraints on external vector stores (must be on-prem or VPC-only?).

Sarah — great, thanks for the numbers. Below are concrete recommendations to address the asks from the demo and to make the dedicated capacity sizing realistic. I tried to keep this actionable for your infra/security teams.

1) SDK setup & Auth- Recommendation: Use Redwood Python SDK (we'll provide Go samples) with OIDC short-lived tokens issued by your IdP + mTLS between the private agents and the dedicated serving tier. Avoid long-lived API keys for production.
- Flow: Service account in your IdP -> short-lived JWT -> exchange for Redwood access token (1h TTL) -> client uses token in Authorization header.
- For provisioning automation we support Terraform + our provisioning API (we'll share snippets).

2) Routing + Fallbacks- Regional routing: route US-East clinical traffic to the nearest regional pool; failover to a lower-cost region if latency SLO is missed.
- Model variants: recommend 2 variants for summarization: small fast model for P95 < 300ms and an LLM variant for fallback or higher-quality batch jobs. Redwood can automatically fallback based on configured SLO thresholds.

3) Structured output & Tool calling- Use the SDK's structured-output helpers (JSON schema enforcement) + tool-calling for EHR update operations. Example contract: {action: redact_phi, fields: [...], confidence_threshold: 0.9}. We will supply example tool connectors for your EHR (HL7/FHIR).
- For PHI redaction keep a local pass (on-prem) before any external feature that might send data out of your VPC.

4) Embedding + Reranker architecture- Query flow: user query -> ANN index (FAISS/HNSW) on private vector store -> top-K candidates (K=50) -> cross-encoder reranker (dedicated model) -> return top-5.
- Indexing: nightly batch reindex (incremental). Use sharded FAISS with per-shard replication for availability.
- Latency: ANN lookup ~5–20ms (depending on shards), reranker model P95 ~50–120ms depending on size. Add this into the total P95 budget.

5) Dedicated capacity sizing (rough numbers based on your QPS)- Assumptions: summarization average tokens ~300; target P95 < 300ms for the fast path; peak 200 QPS.
- Fast summarization variant (quantized): ~1 GPU can support 25–40 QPS depending on model and batching. Initial baseline: 6 GPUs (allows headroom for 200 QPS with batching + KV cache).
- Reranker fleet: cross-encoder requires more compute; plan for 2 dedicated GPUs for reranker to handle 20–40 QPS with headroom.
- Embedding indexing nodes (batch): can be scheduled on spot/backfilling capacity; realtime embedding queries are lightweight — 1 GPU for embedding lookup + CPU for ANN serving.

Autoscale suggestions:
- Scale-up trigger: sustained GPU utilization > 70% for 60s OR average request queue length > 30 for 120s.
- Scale-down: utilization < 30% for 5m and queue length < 5.
- Max cluster size during peak: 12 GPUs (autoscale cap).

Concurrency & Queues:
- Per-GPU concurrency cap: map to model memory and KV cache target (we recommend limiting concurrent generation requests per GPU to 16 for determinism).
- Queueing: Redwood supports a FIFO queuing layer per model with priority tagging; allow clinician-facing traffic higher priority. Use a small emergency fallback capacity for critical low-latency requests.

6) Caching & Batching- Prefix/KV caching for repeated context saves ~25–40% compute for conversational flows. Continuous batching helps throughput but tune target batch windows for P95 latency needs.

Next steps (for workshop):
- We will prepare: GH repo with SDK samples, a 1-page provisioning checklist, and a draft autoscale policy.
- Please confirm: (a) whether vector storage must be on-prem, (b) expected avg token size for summarization, (c) contact for provisioning (email).

I can present this in the Sep 8 workshop. Happy to run a quick sizing spreadsheet with your infra numbers live.

—Karthik

Adding a couple of practical details and a small code snippet you can try in dev:

Snippet (Python SDK, simplified):
from redwood import RedwoodClient
client = RedwoodClient(auth="oidc://<token>")
# structured output enforcement
schema = {"type":"object","properties":{"summary":{"type":"string"}}}
resp = client.generate(model="redwood-fast-summ", prompt=my_prompt, schema=schema, tool_calls=["redact_phi"])

Queueing pattern: place clinician-facing requests in a high-priority queue with a small dedicated pool (2 GPUs) so critical requests never contend with bulk nightly reranks. Bulk re-ranker and batch reindex jobs should be scheduled during off-peak windows and can be preempted by higher-priority traffic.

Provisioning checklist: basic network peering, KMS + key rotation policy, service account provisioning, TLS certificate exchange, firewall rules (I'll attach the checklist).

I attached provisioning-checklist.xlsx and a short list of Terraform snippets for provisioning dedicated nodes in the private VPC. We can hand this to your infra team during the workshop.

—Ben
